newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Mars mission doomed after booster fails.
newsitem.headline: Russian Mars mission doomed after booster fails.

text.p: Russia's hopes of following the United States with a mission to Mars were dashed on Sunday when its space probe ran into trouble hours after liftoff.
Officials said they had lost contact with the $64 million rocket, which failed to break out of the Earth's orbit.

Most of it was expected to re-enter the atmosphere and burn up, although some parts -- possibly including reinforced cannisters of deadly plutonium -- could fall to earth. "The specialists are still working...but it's probably too late," said Vladimir Ananyev, a spokesman for the Russian Space Agency.
An official at the Space Communication Centre in Crimea later told journalists the probe, which had a booster problem, was not likely to last long.
"It will probably soon enter the Earth's atmosphere and cease to exist," Interfax news agency quoted Vladimir Molodtsov, deputy flight manager and head of the control team, as saying.

Russian commercial television channel NTV said parts of the probe could fall to earth and the rocket had four thermoelectric generators fuelled by radioactive plutonium. Space officials were not immediately available to comment.
A nuclear scientist told Reuters such plutonium was highly carcinogenic, but was stored in cannisters designed to withstand the shock of re-entering the atmosphere and hitting the ground.
The probe could spend a maximum of 30 days orbiting Earth, and another official said the team would try to trace it.
"We will carry on looking for it for days," flight manager Konstantin Sukhanov told Reuters by telephone from the centre.
The six-tonne probe lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday at 11.48 p.m. Moscow time (2048 GMT). It had been due to reach Mars on September 12 next year.
Ekho Moskvy radio suggested underfunding of the project might be to blame for the disaster.

Russia's Mars-96 mission was launched two years behind schedule due to cash shortages in the hard-pressed space sector. The probe is carrying 1.1 tonnes of scientific equipment from 20 European countries and the United States.
NTV said incalculable damage had been done to the prestige of Russia's space exploration programme.
"Almost all European states took part in creating the equipment for the station. Germany alone accounts for about 600,000 marks ($400,000)," its commentator said.

Ekho Moskvy radio said scientists working on the project had received government funding only after pressure from the other countries involved. As a result the construction had to be rushed, leaving room for mistakes.
Interfax quoted Molodtsov as saying the fault occurred when booster rockets on the fourth stage failed to ignite.

"Experts think the booster rocket failed in its second ignition while the spacecraft was in the shadow zone (out of contact with Earth). It should have cut in over the Atlantic, in the area of the Gulf of Guinea," the agency said.
Molodtsov told journalists at the Space Communication Centre that the first ignition had succeeded and the craft had then entered the shadow zone.
Contact was re-established after the spacecraft emerged from the shadow zone, but that was 12 minutes later than scheduled. Contact was maintained for three minutes, and then lost.

The mission is the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars in just over a month. The United States launched a robot voyage to the Red Planet two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on December 2.
All were tasked to check for signs of water on the far-away planet -- a key clue to whether there was once life on Mars.
